subject.title: Excommunication and Execution of Father Hidalgo
subject.author: David Alfaro Siqueiros

title: Thirteen Years After the Raid on Trotsky's House
standfirst: In 1940 David Alfaro Siqueiros led an armed raid on Leon Trotsky's house; the guard who let his men in was found dead in a well a month later. Thirteen years on, the Mexican state that had once locked him up over it set him to work instead on this — the execution of the country's own failed revolutionary priest, a century and a half before.

sections.heading: The Raid That Failed, Thirteen Years Before This Picture
sections.body:
Before dawn on 24 May 1940, Siqueiros led roughly twenty men, disguised as police and carrying submachine guns, automatic rifles and incendiary bombs, into Leon Trotsky's compound in Coyoacán. Trotsky later put the number of shots fired into the house at two hundred; the record on his guard Robert Sheldon Harte counts them lower, at just over seventy. Either way it wasn't enough — Trotsky and his wife survived with minor wounds, and their fourteen-year-old grandson took a bullet through the toe.

Harte himself, who had been on gate duty, vanished with the raiders and turned up a month later shot in the head and packed in lime at the bottom of a well. Trotsky had [a plaque made for him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sheldon_Harte) afterward: 'In Memory of Robert Sheldon Harte, 1915–1940, Murdered by Stalin.' Siqueiros was arrested, insisted at trial the whole operation had only ever been meant to get himself expelled from Mexico rather than kill anyone, was never actually tried, and left the country to paint a mural in Chile arranged by the poet Pablo Neruda. Thirteen years later, he painted this.

sections.heading: What Actually Happened to the Priest in the Painting
sections.body:
Miguel Hidalgo was a parish priest who led Mexico's war for independence and lost. Betrayed by the royalist officer Ignacio Elizondo, he was captured at the Wells of Baján on 21 March 1811 and marched to Chihuahua. In Durango that July, Bishop Francisco Gabriel de Olivares formally defrocked and excommunicated him on Inquisition charges that included denying God punishes sin in this life and doubting the Bible's own authenticity; Hidalgo's defence was that he had [never departed from Church doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Hidalgo_y_Costilla) 'in the slightest degree.' A military court convicted him of treason regardless. He was shot by firing squad on 30 July 1811, reportedly telling his executioners, 'Though I may die, I shall be remembered forever; you all will soon be forgotten.' His head, and those of three fellow insurgents, hung from the corners of Guanajuato's Alhóndiga de Granaditas for the next ten years — a warning that helped build the myth instead of ending it.

Independence itself didn't arrive until 1821, a decade after Hidalgo's death, under Agustín de Iturbide, a man who had fought against the rebellion Hidalgo started. The title 'Father of the Nation' was fitted onto him only afterward, by the same church-and-state order that had defrocked and shot him.

sections.heading: An Experimental Workshop, and an Accidental Pollock
sections.body:
In the spring of 1936, running an 'Experimental Workshop' in New York, Siqueiros put down the brush for spray guns, drills and cement applicators and taught what he called [controlled accidents](https://www.thecollector.com/david-alfaro-siqueiros-mexican-muralist-inspired-pollock/) — pouring paint and industrial lacquer straight from the can onto panels laid flat on the floor, then working whatever landed. He framed it as opening a second era of twentieth-century muralism: art made with a factory's tools instead of an easel's.

One of the twenty-four-year-olds in the room was Jackson Pollock. What he took from it — pouring, industrial paint, canvas worked flat on the ground rather than upright — became, a decade on, the vocabulary of his own drip paintings, the ones that turned Abstract Expressionism into a movement. Siqueiros had built the method to serve a collective, didactic art aimed at organising the masses. Handed to Pollock, it produced close to the opposite: one of the most private, individual gestures in twentieth-century American painting.

sections.heading: A State Commission for a Man the State Had Jailed
sections.body:
Between the Trotsky raid and this painting, Siqueiros barely stopped moving through Mexico's prisons and exits. He had already been jailed and exiled once in the early 1930s over his labour organising, and deported from the United States in 1932 for much the same activity. After Chile he came back to Mexico and kept working, and by the early 1950s he was deep into The People to the University, the University to the People, a combined mural, mosaic and relief for the new campus of the National Autonomous University — public, monumental, and paid for by the same government whose police had booked him into [Lecumberri Preventive Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Alfaro_Siqueiros) over an armed plot against a fellow revolutionary barely a decade earlier.

Excommunication and Execution of Father Hidalgo, painted the following year, sits in that same turn: not a private commission or a gallery piece, but a national historical subject handed to an artist the state had rehabilitated into an approved history painter, machine-gun raid and all.

sections.heading: A Man Who Explicitly Hated the Word His Catalogue Uses
sections.body: This feature files the painting under Expressionism, and there's a surface case for it — the firing squad and the crowd around Hidalgo are handled with real physical force, paint pushed hard enough to read as its own kind of violence. But Siqueiros spent his career arguing against roughly what that word usually means. He wanted art that was public, educational and ideological, built to educate the masses and overcome what he called bourgeois, individualist art — the opposite aim of the private, self-expressive gesture the term generally names, including in the American painting his own workshop happened to help invent. If the label fits this canvas at all, it fits the brutality of the scene. It doesn't fit the doctrine of the man who painted it.

sections.heading: What Got Rehabilitated and What Didn't
sections.body:
The rehabilitation had limits. In 1960 Siqueiros was arrested again, this time for publicly attacking President Adolfo López Mateos and backing striking railway workers and teachers, and spent close to four years in prison before international pressure got him pardoned in the spring of 1964. Two years later the Soviet Union gave him the Lenin Peace Prize. He died in Cuernavaca on 6 January 1974, having donated his own house to the state days earlier for use as a museum, and was buried in the Rotunda of Illustrious Persons — the same government that had jailed him repeatedly across five decades filing him, in the end, among its official great men.

It is roughly the arc Hidalgo got, compressed and inverted: a man the state excommunicated and shot became its founding father; a man the state shot at, jailed and exiled kept working until the state gave him a tomb among its own. Neither man had much say in which version of himself the state eventually decided to keep.
